generator.program.note: The lineage's own program (growth plan G2.3a), on the herb base: it gives the values its species leave unset, which the herb program gave as defaults until then.

traits.hypanthium.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 232, 505: Simpson calls the flowers epigynous (perianth on top of the inferior ovary). Simpson p. 505 defines hypogynous and epigynous as flowers without a hypanthium.

traits.note: Reed College's account of the family, with Michigan State's Botany Online and the Sydney eFlora, as search results quote them (the pages themselves were not read): flowers three-merous and zygomorphic; three sepals, one of them dorsal, and three petals, the median one the labellum or lip; in most orchid flowers the ovary twists 180 degrees, bringing the lip to the bottom; stamens, style and stigma joined in one column, usually with one fertile anther (two in the lady's slippers); ovary inferior, of three carpels.

traits.woodiness.note: Hutchinson (vol. 2, 2nd ed., 1959), family 405 Orchidaceae: perennial herbs, on the ground, on trees, or living on fungi; leaves undivided, alternate and often in two ranks, rarely opposite, sometimes all reduced to scales, sheathing at the base.

traits.leaf_division.note: Hutchinson (vol. 2, 2nd ed., 1959), family 405 Orchidaceae: perennial herbs, on the ground, on trees, or living on fungi; leaves undivided, alternate and often in two ranks, rarely opposite, sometimes all reduced to scales, sheathing at the base.

traits.leaf_arrangement.note: Hutchinson (vol. 2, 2nd ed., 1959), family 405 Orchidaceae: perennial herbs, on the ground, on trees, or living on fungi; leaves undivided, alternate and often in two ranks, rarely opposite, sometimes all reduced to scales, sheathing at the base. The books add whorled (sometimes): Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 232, 233, 234: spiral, distichous or whorled.

traits.leaf_habit.note: Watson and Dallwitz, The Families of Flowering Plants (DELTA data, items edited May 2026), family Orchidaceae as that work draws it, there coded together with Apostasiaceae, Cypripediaceae: how long the leaves last (character 37), coded usually deciduous, sometimes evergreen. Read from the coded states by script (spec-rework/b1/delta/mapdelta.py with character 21 added); states the authors do not qualify, side by side, read as often.

traits.rosette.note: Watson and Dallwitz, The Families of Flowering Plants (DELTA data, items edited May 2026), family Orchidaceae as that work draws it, there coded together with Apostasiaceae, Cypripediaceae: whether the leaves gather in rosettes (character 22), coded often a basal rosette, often no rosette. Read from the coded states by script (spec-rework/b1/delta/mapdelta.py with character 21 added); states the authors do not qualify, side by side, read as often.

traits.life_span.note: Watson and Dallwitz, The Families of Flowering Plants (DELTA data, items edited May 2026), family Orchidaceae as that work draws it, there coded together with Apostasiaceae, Cypripediaceae: the herbs' life form (character 21), coded perennial. Read from the coded states by script (spec-rework/b1/delta/mapdelta.py with character 21 added); states the authors do not qualify, side by side, read as often.

traits.leaf_venation.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 232, 233, 234, family Orchidaceae: leaf venation parallel; read as "parallel".

traits.inflorescence.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 232, 233, 234, family Orchidaceae: inflorescence raceme, panicle, spike or solitary; read as {"panicle": "often", "raceme": "often", "solitary": "often", "spike": "often"}.

traits.sexual_system.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 232, 233, 234, family Orchidaceae: sexual system hermaphrodite (rarely unisexual flowers), usually; read as {"hermaphrodite": "usually"}.

traits.fruit_type.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 232, 233, 234, family Orchidaceae: fruit type capsule (loculicidal) (rarely berry), usually; read as {"capsule": "usually"}.

traits.flower_symmetry.note: Added kinds only; the usual kind's source is the family's `traits` note. The books add actinomorphic (rarely): Ingrouille, Diversity and Evolution of Land Plants (1992) p. 176: actinomorphic.
